title: Surface area per unit volume against radius, for a spherical cell
alt: A curve falling steeply from 12 down to 0.25 as radius rises from 0.25 to 12 micrometres, with reference lines at radius 0.5 and radius 10 micrometres.
longDescription: The curve plots three divided by the radius, which is the surface-to-volume ratio of a sphere, against radius in micrometres. At a radius of 0.25 micrometres the ratio is 12 per micrometre. It halves to 6 at 0.5 micrometres, falls to 3 at 1 micrometre, 1.5 at 2, 1 at 3, 0.6 at 5, 0.3 at 10, and 0.25 at 12. The fall is steep on the left and nearly flat on the right, so a change of half a micrometre matters enormously to a bacterium and hardly at all to a human cell. Two reference lines are marked. The first is at radius 0.5 micrometres, the half-width of the rod model of Escherichia coli used in this lesson, where a sphere would give 6 per micrometre; the rod itself gives 5 per micrometre, so shape shifts the answer by less than shape-free size does. The second is at radius 10 micrometres, the half-width of the 20 micrometre sphere used here for a human cell, where the ratio is 0.3 per micrometre. The two marked positions differ by a factor of 20 in radius and about 17 to 20 in the ratio, because the ratio is inversely proportional to radius.

markers.label: 0.5 µm: half-width of the rod model of E. coli
10 µm: half-width of the 20 µm human-cell sphere
